\framekicker{Section 2.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Reading the forward pass}
\begin{isteps}
\item \textbf{Every edge is a weight, and the drawing shows it.} Warm means positive, rose means negative, and thickness is magnitude. A trained network is exactly this picture with different numbers on the edges --- nothing else changes.
\item \textbf{Each unit sums what reaches it, adds a bias, then applies relu.} The sum for the top hidden unit is printed under the figure so you can check it against the inputs and weights shown.
\item \textbf{A unit reading \inlinecode{0} is not broken --- it is \inlinecode{relu} doing its job.} Its sum came out negative and \inlinecode{max(0, z)} clipped it. That unit contributes nothing to this input, and \hilite{a different input would wake it up}.
\item \textbf{The output layer uses softmax}, so its three numbers are positive and sum to 1 --- which is what makes them readable as probabilities.
\end{isteps}
\begin{iband}[signal]
Scale this to 784 inputs, 512 hidden units and 10 outputs and you have the MNIST model from listing 2.2 --- \textbf{401,920 weights on the first layer alone}, every one doing what the four here are doing.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\coursesection{02}{Data representations: tensors}{A container for data. Three attributes, and one special axis.}

\framekicker{Section 2.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Rank, shape, dtype}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\linewidth,height=0.56\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/ch02-tensor-ranks.tex.pdf}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont The same four numbers 7, 2, 9, 4 appear at every rank. What changes is how many indices it takes to reach one of them.\par}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 2.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Reading the drawing: what each rank actually is}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Every tensor has exactly three defining attributes: its \textbf{number of axes} (rank), its \textbf{shape}, and its \textbf{dtype}. Everything else follows from those.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{itable}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.094\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.1504\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.1504\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.2444\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.3008\textwidth}}
\thead{Rank} & \thead{Name} & \thead{Shape} & \thead{To reach one number} & \thead{Example} \\ \midrule
0 & scalar & \inlinecode{()} & \inlinecode{t} & a loss value --- one number per batch \\
1 & vector & \inlinecode{(4,)} & \inlinecode{t[i]} & one MNIST image after flattening is \inlinecode{(784,)} \\
2 & matrix & \inlinecode{(3, 4)} & \inlinecode{t[i][j]} & a batch of flattened images, \inlinecode{(128, 784)} \\
3 & tensor & \inlinecode{(2, 3, 4)} & \inlinecode{t[i][j][k]} & a batch of images before flattening, \inlinecode{(128, 28, 28)} \\
\end{itable}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}\textbf{Rank is a count of axes, not a size.} A \inlinecode{(60000, 28, 28)} tensor and a \inlinecode{(2, 3, 4)} tensor are both rank 3, and every rule you learn about one applies to the other. \hilite{That is the whole reason the abstraction is worth having.}\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{iband}[signal]
The word \textit{dimension} is used for two different things and causes real confusion: a rank-3 tensor has \textbf{3 axes}, while a \inlinecode{(784,)} vector is often called \textit{784-dimensional}. Say \textbf{rank} for axes and \textbf{shape} for sizes, and the ambiguity disappears.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 2.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Reading them off a real tensor}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}MNIST before preprocessing is a rank-3 tensor: 60,000 images, each a 28$\times$28 grid of 8-bit grayscale values.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{the three attributes}{listings/ch02-11.py}
\ioutput{listings/ch02-12.txt}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 2.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The terminology trap that costs people an afternoon}
\begin{iband}[rose]
A \textbf{5-dimensional vector} is not a \textbf{5-dimensional tensor}. The first has \hilite{one axis holding five numbers}; the second has \hilite{five axes}
\end{iband}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Misreading this makes shape error messages unintelligible, and shape errors are the most common failure you will hit in the exercises.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 2.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Slicing tensors}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Selecting part of a tensor uses the same bracket syntax as NumPy. A colon means \textit{all of this axis}, and negative indices count from the end.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 2.7--2.8 --- slices}{listings/ch02-13.py}
\ioutput{listings/ch02-14.txt}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 2.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The batch axis is always axis 0}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Models are not trained on whole datasets; they are trained on small \textbf{batches}. Cutting a batch is just a slice along the first axis.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 2.9 --- batches}{listings/ch02-15.py}
\ioutput{listings/ch02-16.txt}
\begin{iband}[signal]
Axis 0 is the \textbf{samples axis} --- and because of batching it is also called the \textbf{batch axis}. \hilite{Every shape error you will read starts with identifying this axis.}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\begin{itable}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.188\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.0752\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.282\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.3948\textwidth}}
\thead{Kind of data} & \thead{Rank} & \thead{Shape} & \thead{Example from the book} \\ \midrule

{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}An element-wise operation applies independently to each entry --- which is precisely why it parallelises so well. Written out as loops, \inlinecode{relu} is this:\par}\vskip 4pt

{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}In practice you never write those loops. NumPy expresses the identical computation in two lines --- and the difference is not cosmetic.\par}\vskip 4pt

Roughly \textbf{100$\times$}, and it is not a language effect. NumPy hands the work to BLAS routines written in C and Fortran; on a GPU the same operation runs as \hilite{fully vectorised CUDA}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 2.3.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Broadcasting: fitting a small shape to a big one}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth,height=0.60\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/ch02-broadcast.tex.pdf}
\end{center}

{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}No memory is actually duplicated --- the repetition is \hilite{algorithmic, not physical}\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 2.3.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The rule, and where it quietly goes wrong}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Broadcasting applies when one tensor has shape \inlinecode{(a, b, \ldots{}, n, n+1, \ldots{}, m)} and the other has \inlinecode{(n, n+1, \ldots{}, m)}.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 2.11 --- broadcasting in anger}{listings/ch02-20.py}
\ioutput{listings/ch02-21.txt}
\begin{iband}[amber]
This is the most common source of \textbf{silent} bugs: the shapes line up, the code runs, and the \hilite{meaning is wrong}. When a result looks strange, print the shapes first.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 2.3.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The tensor product, and its one compatibility rule}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}The tensor product --- \inlinecode{matmul}, or the \inlinecode{@} operator --- is the operation that actually combines features. It has exactly one rule you must remember.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{matmul}{listings/ch02-22.py}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Visually: line the two up as rectangles --- \hilite{the width of the first must match the height of the second}\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 2.3.4}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Reshaping rearranges; it never invents or destroys}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}A reshape changes how the same coefficients are laid out. The total count is unchanged, which is why it is cheap.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 2.12 --- reshape and transpose}{listings/ch02-23.py}
\ioutput{listings/ch02-24.txt}
\begin{iband}[signal]
This is exactly what \inlinecode{train\_images.reshape((60000, 784))} did in the first example: \hilite{the pixels never changed, only their arrangement}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 2.3.5}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Every tensor operation is a geometric one}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\linewidth,height=0.56\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/ch02-geom-ops.tex.pdf}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont One shape, four operations. The dashed outline is where it started.\par}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 2.3.5}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Reading the drawing: what moved, and what did it}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Treat the numbers in a tensor as \textbf{coordinates}. Then every operation in the previous slide is a movement, and the matrix is the instruction for the movement.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{itable}{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.2068\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.4324\textwidth}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.3008\textwidth}}
\thead{Operation} & \thead{What it does to the shape} & \thead{Written as} \\ \midrule
\textbf{Translation} & Slides it. Every point moves by the same vector; nothing turns or stretches. & \inlinecode{y = x + b} \\
\textbf{Rotation} & Turns it about the origin. Lengths and angles survive --- the shape is the same shape, pointing elsewhere. & \inlinecode{y = R @ x} \\
\textbf{Scaling} & Stretches each axis by its own factor. Here x by 1.5 and y by 0.6, which is why it comes out squat. & \inlinecode{y = D @ x} \\
\textbf{Affine} & Any matrix, then a vector. Straight lines stay straight and parallel lines stay parallel --- but angles do not survive. & \inlinecode{y = W @ x + b} \\
\end{itable}
\begin{iband}[signal]
\textbf{A \inlinecode{Dense} layer is the fourth row.} \inlinecode{W @ x + b} is an affine transform, and nothing else. A stack of them with no activation between is still one affine transform --- which is the next slide, and the reason activations exist.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 2.3.5}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Why an activation function is not optional}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}A \inlinecode{Dense} layer without an activation computes \inlinecode{y = W @ x + b} --- an affine transform. Chain two of them and expand:\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{two affine layers collapse into one}{listings/ch02-25.py}
\begin{iband}[rose]
So a deep stack of \inlinecode{Dense} layers with no activation is \hilite{secretly a single linear model}, however many layers you give it. Nonlinearities such as \inlinecode{relu} are what make the hypothesis space rich.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}
\note{If a product manager takes one thing from chapter 2, this is it: without nonlinearity, depth buys nothing at all.}

\framekicker{Section 2.3.5}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Deep learning as uncrumpling a paper ball}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Chollet's image for what a deep network does: complicated, folded data \textbf{manifolds} are gradually pulled apart until the classes separate cleanly.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{iband}[signal]
It happens through a long series of \textbf{small, elementary geometric moves} --- like uncrumpling a paper ball with successive finger movements. \hilite{Each layer disentangles the data a little.}
\end{iband}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Chapter 5 makes this precise, under the name of the \textit{manifold hypothesis}.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\coursesection{04}{The engine: gradient-based optimisation}{Derivatives, gradients, SGD, and the chain rule.}

\framekicker{Section 2.4}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The training loop, and which step is hard}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth,height=0.60\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/ch02-loop4.tex.pdf}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont Four steps, repeated over batches. Only the fourth is difficult.\par}
\begin{iband}[amber]
Tuning each coefficient by hand is impossible --- modern networks have \hilite{millions to billions of parameters}. Gradient descent solves for all of them at once.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 2.4.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{A derivative is the slope of a local approximation}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}For a smooth function, a small change in \inlinecode{x} produces a small change in \inlinecode{y}. Near a point, \inlinecode{f(x + $\varepsilon$) $\approx$ y + a$\cdot$$\varepsilon$}, and that \inlinecode{a} is the \textbf{derivative}.\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{ibullets}
\item \inlinecode{a} negative $\rightarrow$ increasing \inlinecode{x} \textbf{decreases} \inlinecode{f(x)}.
\item \inlinecode{a} positive $\rightarrow$ increasing \inlinecode{x} \textbf{increases} \inlinecode{f(x)}.
\item Its magnitude says how fast the change happens.
\end{ibullets}
\begin{iband}[signal]
So to make \inlinecode{f} smaller, move \inlinecode{x} \hilite{in the direction opposite its derivative}. That single sentence is the whole of optimisation.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 2.4.2}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{A gradient is a derivative for tensors}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Hold the data fixed, and the loss becomes a function of the weights alone: \inlinecode{loss\_value = f(W)}.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{what the gradient is a gradient of}{listings/ch02-26.py}
\begin{iband}[signal]
To lower the loss, step against the gradient: \inlinecode{W1 = W0 - step * grad(f(W0), W0)}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 2.4.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Why this is done by iteration and not by solving}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Minima occur where the derivative is zero. So why not just solve \inlinecode{grad(f(W), W) = 0} directly?\par}\vskip 4pt
\begin{iband}[rose]
Because for a network with millions of parameters that is \hilite{analytically intractable}. Iteration is not a shortcut; it is the only available route.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 2.4.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Mini-batch stochastic gradient descent}
\begin{isteps}
\item Draw a \textbf{random} batch of samples and targets. (The word \textit{stochastic} comes from this randomness.)
\item Forward pass $\rightarrow$ predictions.
\item Compute the loss.
\item \textbf{Backward pass} $\rightarrow$ gradient of the loss with respect to the parameters.
\item \inlinecode{W -= learning\_rate * gradient}.
\end{isteps}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Repeat. Each step lowers the loss a little; enough steps and the model fits.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 2.4.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Seven steps of it, on a real curve}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.97\linewidth,height=0.56\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/ch02-sgd-walk.tex.pdf}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont Cyan: the slope measured at that point. Amber: the step taken because of it.\par}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 2.4.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Reading the walk: three things to notice}
\begin{isteps}
\item \textbf{The step is the slope, scaled.} Nothing decides how far to move except \inlinecode{learning\_rate $\times$ gradient}. Where the curve is steep the step is long; where it flattens the step shortens \hilite{on its own}. No schedule does that --- it falls out of the rule.
\item \textbf{It never lands exactly on the minimum,} and it does not need to. Training stops when the loss stops improving, not when the gradient reaches zero.
\item \textbf{Only the local slope is known.} At every point the walk sees the tangent and nothing else --- not the shape of the curve, not where the minimum is. That is why a bad learning rate is fatal: the step is taken blind.
\end{isteps}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}The arithmetic beside the curve is the whole algorithm. \inlinecode{w $\leftarrow$ w $-$ lr $\cdot$ dL/dw}, five times, with real numbers you can check on paper. \textbf{Everything else in this chapter is about computing that one derivative efficiently} for millions of parameters at once.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 2.4.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Learning rate: the one number that decides whether it works}
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.3253\textwidth}
\begin{icardwarn}
\cardh{Too small}
Convergence crawls --- many steps for very little progress. It can look as though training has stalled.
\end{icardwarn}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.3253\textwidth}
\begin{icardbad}
\cardh{Too large}
Updates overshoot wildly; the loss jumps around and \hilite{never comes down}.
\end{icardbad}
\end{minipage}%
\hfill
\begin{minipage}[t]{0.3253\textwidth}
\begin{icardgood}
\cardh{Momentum}
Update using the current gradient \textbf{and} previous updates --- like a ball rolling downhill with enough speed to cross a shallow dip.
\end{icardgood}
\end{minipage}%
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}The variants that improve on plain SGD are called \textbf{optimizers}: SGD with momentum, Adagrad, RMSprop, Adam.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 2.4.4}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{The chain rule, applied backwards over a graph}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth,height=0.60\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/ch02-graph.tex.pdf}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont Solid arrows are the forward pass; dashed arrows are the backward pass, each carrying one local derivative.\par}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Multiply the local derivatives along a path and you have the gradient. Applying the chain rule this way over a network \textbf{is} backpropagation.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 2.4.5}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Two details that make the graph work}
\begin{ibullets}
\item When there are \textbf{several paths} from node \inlinecode{a} to node \inlinecode{b}, the contributions of the paths are \hilite{summed}.
\item A \textbf{computation graph} is a directed acyclic graph of operations. It makes computation itself into data --- a structure a machine can read and manipulate.
\end{ibullets}
\begin{iband}[signal]
Modern frameworks walk that graph for you. That is \textbf{automatic differentiation}, and it is why \hilite{you will never write backpropagation by hand}
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 2.4.5}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Autodiff in three lines}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}TensorFlow records operations inside a \inlinecode{GradientTape} scope, then replays them backwards on request.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 2.19 --- a first derivative}{listings/ch02-27.py}
\ioutput{listings/ch02-28.txt}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}The answer is 2, which is what you would get by hand --- except nothing here was told the rule for differentiating a line.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 2.4.5}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{\ldots{}and a second derivative, which is a physics answer}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Tapes can be nested: the inner one differentiates the position, the outer one differentiates that result again.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 2.20 --- nested tapes}{listings/ch02-29.py}
\ioutput{listings/ch02-30.txt}
\begin{iband}[signal]
\inlinecode{position = 4.9$\cdot$t$^{2}$} is free fall. Its second derivative is the \hilite{acceleration due to gravity}, and autodiff returned 9.8 without ever being given the formula.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\coursesection{05}{Rewriting the first example from scratch}{No fit(), no built-in Dense. The result has to hold up.}

\framekicker{Section 2.6}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{What we are about to rebuild}
\begin{center}
\includegraphics[width=0.92\linewidth,height=0.60\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figs/ch02-scratch.tex.pdf}
\end{center}
\vskip 3pt{\color{ink3}\fontsize{7.4}{9.4}\selectfont Four small classes and one function replace Sequential, Dense, and fit() between them.\par}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 2.6.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{A layer, written out}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}A \inlinecode{Dense} layer owns two weights and applies one transformation. That is the entire class.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 2.21 --- NaiveDense}{listings/ch02-31.py}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}\inlinecode{W} starts random and \inlinecode{b} starts at zero --- exactly the starting condition chapter 1 described.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 2.6.1}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{A model is just layers, applied in order}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}With a layer in hand, a model needs to do only two things: call the layers in sequence, and expose all their weights together so the optimizer can reach them.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 2.22 --- NaiveSequential}{listings/ch02-32.py}
\begin{iband}[signal]
Note how little there is to it: a model is \hilite{a list of layers and a for loop}. Everything else in Keras is convenience on top.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 2.6.2 -- 2.6.3}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{One training step is the four figures, in code}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Forward pass, loss, gradients, update --- the same four moves as the loop diagram, now with a real optimizer.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 2.24 --- one\_training\_step}{listings/ch02-33.py}
\begin{iband}[signal]
Four lines, four ideas: \hilite{forward, loss, gradients, update}. Every training loop in the rest of the book is a variation on this shape.
\end{iband}
\end{frame}

\framekicker{Section 2.6.4}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{And the loop around it}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Wrapping that single step in two loops --- over epochs, and over batches within an epoch --- is all that \inlinecode{fit()} does underneath.\par}\vskip 4pt
\icode{python}{listing 2.26 --- fit, by hand}{listings/ch02-34.py}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}\inlinecode{BatchGenerator} is a dozen lines that hand out consecutive slices --- the batch axis from section 2.2, put to work.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}

\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{Does it work? Run it and see}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}Assemble the same two-layer network out of the hand-written parts, train it for ten epochs, and score it the same way the built-in version was scored.\par}\vskip 4pt

\framekicker{Section 2.6.5}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{90\% versus 97.8\% --- and why that is the lesson}
\begin{iband}[amber]
The hand-written version scores \textbf{lower}, and that is not a bug. It uses plain SGD at \inlinecode{learning\_rate=1e-3}; the first example used \hilite{\textbf{Adam}}
\end{iband}
{\fontsize{9.4}{12.6}\selectfont\color{fg2}So the gap measures \textbf{the choice of optimizer}, not the quality of the implementation. It is one of the clearest demonstrations in the book of how much that choice is worth.\par}\vskip 4pt
\end{frame}
\note{This slide is misread more than any other in the chapter. State plainly that the lower number does not mean the manual code is wrong.}

\framekicker{Summary}
\begin{frame}[shrink=25]{What has to survive this chapter}
\begin{isteps}
\item \textbf{Tensors} are containers with \textbf{rank, shape, dtype}. Axis 0 is the samples axis, and therefore the batch axis.
\item \textbf{Tensor operations are geometric.} A Dense layer without an activation is an affine transform, and stacking those still gives an affine transform.
\item \textbf{Learning} means finding weight values that minimise the loss on the training data.
\item \textbf{Mini-batch SGD} updates weights from gradients computed on random batches.
\item \textbf{Chain rule + autodiff = backpropagation}, carried out over a computation graph.
\item \textbf{Loss} measures success at the task; \textbf{optimizer} decides how the descent is performed --- and that choice is worth several points of accuracy.
\end{isteps}
\vskip 4pt
